name: Samosa
subtitle: crisp pastry triangles with a spiced potato and pea filling
prepNotes: The pastry is short, not soft: rub plenty of oil into the flour until it holds a shape when squeezed. That is what makes it crisp rather than chewy.
Fry low and slow. Samosas dropped into hot oil blister and go soft within minutes.

steps.text: Rub 6 tbsp of the oil and the ajwain into the maida until the mixture holds together when pressed in your fist.
steps.tip: This test matters. Too little fat and the crust will be tough.

steps.text: Add cold water sparingly to make a stiff dough. Knead only until smooth, then rest 30 minutes covered.
steps.tip: Stiff, not soft. A soft dough gives bubbles and a wavy shell.

steps.text: For the filling, crackle cumin in 2 tbsp oil, add ginger and chilli, then the peas and a splash of water, and cook until tender.
Add the crushed potato, coriander powder, amchur, garam masala, fennel and salt. Cook 4 minutes and cool completely.
steps.tip: Warm filling makes the pastry damp and it splits in the oil.

steps.text: Roll a ball of dough into an oval, cut it in half, form a cone from each, fill, and seal the edge with a wet finger, pressing firmly.
steps.tip: Any gap and the samosa drinks oil.

steps.text: Rest the shaped samosas 15 minutes uncovered so the surface dries.
Fry at 140C, low, for 10 minutes until pale and blistering slowly, then raise to 180C for 3 minutes to colour.
steps.tip: The low first fry sets the layers. Straight into hot oil gives a bubbled, greasy shell.

steps.text: Drain and serve with tamarind and mint chutneys.

storage: Best within a few hours. Fried samosas keep a day and revive in a hot oven, never a microwave. Shaped uncooked samosas freeze for a month and fry from frozen.
